title: TEAM Changes Where the Revenue Cycle Ends
summary: TEAM changes where Revenue Cycle responsibility ends by requiring cross-functional ownership, coordinated handoffs, and visibility across the full episode of care.
body_markdown:
For years, Revenue Cycle leaders have largely measured success around getting a claim out cleanly, getting it paid, and preventing denials. The Transforming Episode Accountability Model (TEAM) pushes us to think beyond the individual claim and look at the full episode of care.


That changes where Revenue Cycle responsibility ends.


Hospitals generally have visibility into discharge planning, outpatient follow-up, and the financial impact of care after an inpatient stay. The bigger challenge is making sure those efforts are coordinated—and that every team involved has the information it needs, including payer requirements and authorization requirements for both inpatient and outpatient services.


## TEAM Requires More Than a Finance Workstream


TEAM should not be treated as a project that belongs only to Finance, Revenue Cycle, Case Management, or IT. It crosses too many operational areas.


Utilization Management and Case Management should play a central role in coordinating patient care and planning with the payer. Patient Access needs visibility into eligibility and authorization requirements. Coding and CDI need to support accurate clinical representation. Revenue Cycle needs to understand what happened across the episode and how it ultimately affected reimbursement.


Clinical and physician leadership, discharge planning, IT, outpatient teams, and post-acute partners also need a seat at the table.


And I would include frontline staff in the design process. They are often the people who can tell you where the handoffs actually break—not where we think they break based on a workflow diagram.


## Someone Has to Coordinate the Whole Program


If an organization has the resources, I would strongly consider assigning a dedicated operational project or program manager to coordinate TEAM readiness and implementation.


That does not mean the project manager owns every workflow. Department leaders still need to own their respective responsibilities.


**The project manager owns the coordination.**


That distinction is important. This is not an IT project manager simply overseeing system changes. It is an operational leader who can see across departments, track dependencies, identify gaps, and make sure decisions turn into actual workflow changes.


If a dedicated project manager is not feasible, an existing operational leader can fill that role—but that person needs enough authority and visibility to hold teams accountable across the organization.


## Map the Episode Before You Measure It


One of the first things I would do is map the entire episode from admission through discharge and post-discharge care.


For every major step, define:


- Who owns it
- What information is required
- When the work must happen
- What the payer requires
- Who receives the handoff


That exercise may sound basic, but unclear ownership is one of the easiest ways for a process to fail.


Ideally, there should be very little follow-up required to determine who was supposed to do what. If responsibilities and workflows are clearly defined upfront, teams should know when they need to obtain information, when they need to provide it, and who owns the next step.


## Revenue Cycle Needs Visibility Across the Episode


The operational lead should be able to monitor the pieces that ultimately affect both patient care and financial performance: eligibility confirmation, required notifications, authorizations, discharge and post-acute planning, denials, readmissions, episode costs, and payment variances.


That does not mean Revenue Cycle owns all of those functions. It means we need enough visibility to understand how an upstream decision or missed handoff eventually affects the financial outcome.


When a claim is delayed or denied, I do not want the organization to stop at the denial reason. I want us to go upstream and ask where the workflow broke and who owned that step.


## A Workflow That Works Today May Not Work Tomorrow


One of the biggest risks I see with TEAM—and with major Revenue Cycle changes in general—is assuming existing workflows are good enough.


Organizations can spend significant time designing a process and still miss something if they do not have the right stakeholders involved or if they fail to keep the workflow current as regulations and payer requirements change.


**A compliant workflow today does not automatically remain compliant tomorrow.**


There needs to be a repeatable process for monitoring changes and translating them into operations:


**Regulatory or payer change → Operational impact → Workflow/system update → Staff communication and training → Validation**


That last piece—validation—is important. Sending an email or updating a policy does not mean the change was successfully implemented.


## Success Still Comes Back to the Basics


From a Revenue Cycle perspective, some of the clearest indicators of success remain familiar: clean claims, prompt payment, and fewer preventable denials.


TEAM adds a broader episode-level financial view, and organizations will need to understand performance across that full episode. But I would not lose sight of the operational basics while building more sophisticated measures.


If we see a denial, delay, readmission, payment variance, or unexpected episode cost, the question should be:


**Where did the process break?**


Then we need to trace that issue back through the workflow rather than treating the financial outcome as an isolated event.


## TEAM Changes the Handoff


The biggest shift may not be a new metric or a new technology. It may be the expectation that hospitals manage the episode as a connected operational process instead of a series of departmental transactions.


That requires clear ownership, coordinated handoffs, current payer and regulatory requirements, strong communication, and someone looking across the entire program to make sure the pieces stay connected.


Revenue Cycle does not need to own every step.


**But we do need to understand how every step affects the outcome.**
